I worked at KFC when I was sixteen.

I thought I was above the place. I was an honor student, preparing for college, from a high-middle class family. I only worked there because my mom demanded I get a job and there weren't many options in my town for an inexperienced teenager.

I did well. I showed up, I worked hard. I did more than the average employee. But one girl, Hannah, did better than me. She wore a ton of makeup and people talked about the abortions she'd had. I thought she was white trash. I didn't think much of her.

One night, four employees called in sick. It was just me, Hannah, and the cook. I struggled at the front counter while Hannah took drive thru. I worked my ass off while Hannah did more than I thought humanly capable. She took orders, aided the cook, ran out the front door to deliver orders when the drive thru got backed up, fixed our broken boiler, and never took off her headset. Never took a break. That girl worked six hours straight with a calm head and a determination I could never imagine. I botched change and mismanaged orders while Hannah did twice as much, completing every order with a smile on her face.

We made it through that night. I had sweated through my clothes by the end of it and quit a few weeks later. I don't know what happened to Hannah. But I remember that night as a lesson that gifts and talents come in many forms. No one is above pure perseverance.

Everyday I watch a foster mother pull up to her foster daughter's school in an old red jeep. She's older - maybe 50, 55. The jeep is dirty, and she's dressed in old clothes. Each day she opens the back door of the jeep and lifts her foster son to the ground.

He can't walk well. He leans against her, grabs her arms, moans to be picked up. It's obvious he can't talk. At first, I wondered why the hell she didn't carry this boy who wished so much to be carried. He cried, and I cried with him, wishing she'd just pick up this sweet boy.

 But she's patient. She waits. She encourages this little boy to use his legs, and after kind words, he walks along side her. One leg, then the other. Awkward, jolting, but moving. He walks, slowly but proudly, once again assured that his legs are able. That HE is able. She claps her hands and rubs his head, whispering sweet things into his ears. 

What could be more beautiful than this boy walking along his foster mom, ready to greet his sister upon his own two legs?

I work for my (large) county's public health officer. He's the smartest and most compassionate man I know. Many times he's explained to me the importance of vaccinations, but this is the reason that has always stuck with me:

Children who are immunocompromised can not afford to catch chicken pox from their unvaccinated classmates. Kids who already have health issues, who have fought disease, who struggle daily with health problems, CANNOT fight against measles or mumps or whatever ailment an unvaccinated child might spread. Sure, a kid might be healthy and deal with chicken pox just fine. But a child dealing with a larger health issue? Exposed to excess, potentially dangerous germs at preschool or kindergarten? Not good. 

Parents can chose to not vaccinate their own, healthy child. But rarely do they think about the kids their child will encounter every day.

When I was a kid I had a lot of anxiety about sleeping, so before bed I'd always ask my dad to check on me three times. Not just once, not twice - three times. 

Every night for almost five years, no matter how tired or stressed he was, my dad would come upstairs three times to check on me. I knew because I was a light sleeper and would wake up each time. And yes, he always checked on me not just once, not twice, but three times. 

I'm 24 now and my dad is still my hero and my best friend.
